source: Nuxoll & Laird (2012) Enhancing intelligent agents with episodic memory, Cognitive Systems Research 17-18:34-48
finding: Soar got a task-independent episodic memory. Each episode is a snapshot of working memory, stored automatically, and only changes are stored. The agent must build a cue on purpose to retrieve. The best match is rebuilt in a reserved area, with a time index and a match score, and the agent can step to the next or previous episode.
numbers: New episode encoded each time the agent acts in the world; recording every cycle instead 'had little impact on performance'. Working memory elements below an activation threshold are left out. Match score = cardinality of shared elements plus activation of matched elements. Below a threshold, retrieval fails.
quote: encoding is automatic; retrieval is deliberate
limits: Memory has no forgetting, consolidation, generalisation across episodes, or model of time (authors say so). Soar 8 version; Soar 9 later dropped activation-biased retrieval for speed.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S0 class record: automatic write, deliberate cue, best-match read, next/previous step, plus a failure signal when nothing matches.

source: Nuxoll & Laird (2012), section 7.1 action modeling (Eaters)
finding: Episodic memory alone let an Eaters agent predict what each move would score. It cued with state plus proposed move, got the best match, then asked for the next episode to read the score change. It picks the move with the best predicted change.
numbers: 16x16 grid, food worth 5 or 10. Five runs, averaged, window 10. Accuracy started at a high failure rate and rose toward perfect prediction as memories accumulated (graph only, no table of values).
limits: Toy domain. Failed retrievals count as failures. Wrong results possible when the retrieved memory is only a near match.
agent_relevance: A cheap forward model built from stored past outcomes, no training. A scaffold could keep (state, action, outcome) triples and retrieve the nearest one before choosing an operator.

source: Nuxoll & Laird (2012), section 7.2 decision-making from past experience (TankSoar)
finding: A TankSoar agent used episodic memory in place of hand-written attack rules. It evaluated each action by retrieving a similar past episode and replaying up to ten following episodes, then scored the net change in game score with a discount favouring recent steps. It learned to beat the hand-coded control agent over successive games.
numbers: 10 repetitions, 95% confidence bars on margin of victory. Between 200 and 700 actions available per step. Three tactics emerged: dodge short-range missiles, back away while firing, break line of sight when losing. Margin started negative (a loss) and became positive. Exact margin not tabled.
limits: Authors: gains rely on consistent outcomes; where outcomes were unreliable, behavior was more variable. Only the Attack mode was replaced.
agent_relevance: Shows long-horizon value can be read off episode chains (what happened next), not only the next step. For us: store trajectories, not just facts.

source: Nuxoll & Laird (2012), section 7.3 retroactive learning and 7.4 boosting chunking
finding: After acting randomly, the agent paused, queried its episodes for every neighbour-cell pattern, and used chunking to write rules. It then behaved near ideal. Separately, chunking the results of episodic decisions removed later retrievals and made the agent eat faster per decision cycle.
numbers: Five runs each. Retroactive learning reached near-ideal accuracy (last-10-actions metric); remaining errors were novel situations with no analog. Chunked episodic agent beat unchunked agent in score per decision cycle, called statistically significant, no p-value given.
limits: Authors warn: in stochastic settings the eager learner can compile wrong answers from the episodic store. Small state space with consistent outcomes.
agent_relevance: Pattern for our loop: log raw episodes cheaply, then offline 'rest' step distils them into rules. Caches built on noisy episodes can lock in errors, so test before promoting.

source: Nuxoll & Laird (2012), section 7.5 virtual sensing (TankSoar battery search)
finding: Blind tank used episodic recall of 'where I saw the battery from here' to build chains of paths to the battery, and found it about ten times faster than random search.
numbers: Log-scale y-axis, moves to reach battery fell as episodes accumulated; authors state 'an order of magnitude faster than a random search'.
limits: Paths are not optimal. Depends on being able to reconstruct the needed knowledge from stored episodes.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping an event log the agent can query for facts it did not note at the time.

source: Nuxoll & Laird (2004) A cognitive model of episodic memory integrated with a general cognitive architecture, ICCM
finding: First Soar episodic memory (Soar-EM). Matching by count of shared features gave only a small gain over random. Biasing the match by working-memory activation (recency and frequency of use) lifted the eater up to greedy-agent level.
numbers: Each state has 31-36 features, only 2 decide the right move. Five iterations of 1500 internal decisions (about 130 world actions) per run, five runs averaged. Unbiased matching: slightly above random. Activation-biased: comparable to the greedy upper bound. Authors estimate over 1 quadrillion possible inputs.
limits: Worst-case retrieval linear in number of episodes. Single toy domain. Cue differing by one feature (the move) is swamped by other matching features.
agent_relevance: Key finding: unweighted similarity retrieval is drowned by irrelevant features. Cue should name only the few features that matter; weight by what was active.

source: Gorski & Laird (2011) Learning to use episodic memory, Cognitive Systems Research 12:144-153 (ICCM 2009 version read)
finding: Soar's reinforcement learning can learn when to retrieve, which cue to use, whether to step to the next episode, and how to build a cue from several features, while learning to act at the same time. Plain RL cannot solve these tasks.
numbers: Well World: external action -1, internal action -0.1, thirsty step -2, safety +2, satisfied thirst +8. 250 trials averaged, Hanning-smoothed. Exp1 single cue: reaches optimal, slower with 5 distracter cues. Exp2 temporal: asymptote after about 4,500 actions, often not fully optimal. Exp3 conjunctive cues: optimal, slower with 2 distracters.
limits: Toy domain. Exploration noise hurts performance while learning. In exp2 every trial converged either to the optimal policy or to a 'toggle a bit' policy that uses retrieval as a flag.
agent_relevance: Memory-use policy can be learned, but it is a hard, partly observable problem. If we want the agent to learn when to consult memory, expect slow, unreliable learning unless seeded by instruction.

source: Gorski & Laird (2011), Table 1: exploration decay vs convergence
finding: How long random exploration decays changes whether the agent finds the best memory policy. The table lists percent of trials that converged to the optimal memory control policy for fixed vs deliberate advance, at 500, 5,000 and 50,000 steps of decay.
numbers: Values printed in the extracted text (layout garbled): fixed advance 26% / 71% / 38%; deliberate advance 60% / 25% / 36% at 500 / 5,000 / 50,000 steps. Reading of which number belongs to which cell is uncertain.
limits: Column assignment is uncertain because the PDF text is scrambled. Authors only conclude that exploration decay interacts with learning and needs future work.
agent_relevance: Warning that convergence rates swing widely with a single schedule parameter. Treat any learned memory-use policy as fragile.

source: Wallace, Dickinson & Nuxoll (2013) Hashing for lightweight episodic recall, AAAI Spring Symposium on Lifelong Machine Learning
finding: ZigguSoar watches rule reward variance, and when a rule's reward is inconsistent it specialises the rule on a short history taken from a hashed episodic store. This lets Soar RL learn in a hidden-state environment (Flip) where baseline RL fails, without full episodic retrieval.
numbers: Flip environment, 20 runs, 100-step moving average, first 10,000 steps. Baseline learns only the deterministic Up prediction. ZigguSoar learns both Up and Left predictions. Rule count grows without bound because no finite history is enough. Full Soar episodic matching about 50 ms with 1M episodes over 14 hours (Derbinsky & Laird 2009, cited).
limits: Assumes deterministic environment so variance means bad state representation. Only one small environment. Authors say methods are early predecessors of newer hidden-state methods. URL is the likely AAAI SSS 2013 page; the PDF was read from a local copy.
agent_relevance: Idea: detect that a rule is unreliable (high variance of outcomes) and then add context. That is a signal-driven doubt trigger, matching guardrail G1.

source: Derbinsky, Li & Laird (2012) Algorithms for scaling in a general episodic memory, AAMAS extended abstract
finding: A new cue-matching index in Soar keeps real-time retrieval for very long lives. Retrieval time grows with the age of the thing being sought.
numbers: Soar 9.3.1. Over 100 cues across 44 planning-domain instances, word-sense disambiguation, 3 video games and a robot. 12 hours of robot run: baseline encoded over 58 million episodes, variant nearly 109 million. Max cue-match time grew 3.6x slower (before a task shift) and 4.9x slower (after). Baseline passed 50 ms in under 12 hours; variant projected to stay under 50 ms for about 694M episodes (more than 3 days).
limits: Projection is an extrapolation. Hardware: Xeon L5520. 50 ms threshold is a convention for reactivity. Variant did not greatly change most tasks. URL is the proceedings index; the PDF was read from a local copy.
agent_relevance: Retrieval cost for old items rises with store size. For an LLM scaffold, keep the record small and indexed, and prefer recent or cued items.

source: Soar Manual 9.6+ (2017-), chapter 5 Reinforcement Learning
finding: Soar RL tunes numeric preferences on operators. An RL rule has a single numeric-indifferent preference on a proposed operator. Q is the sum of all matching RL rules, i.e. a linear approximator with binary features. Updates run on Sarsa or Q-learning at each selected RL operator. Reward comes via a reward-link on each state.
numbers: Defaults: learning rate alpha 0.3, discount gamma 0.9. Sarsa delta = alpha[r + gamma Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]. Eligibility traces off by default (decay 0). Default exploration is softmax, manual advises epsilon-greedy or Boltzmann. Rules can be made by the gp command; learning applies in every substate (hierarchical RL).
limits: Manual, not an experiment. No performance numbers. RL only changes selection among operators already proposed.
agent_relevance: RL here only breaks ties among legal operators after symbolic knowledge has run out. That matches our 'code selects, model fills a slot' split, with learned preferences used only when rules are silent.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture, section 5 RL
finding: RL influences selection only when other preferences cannot decide. Hard-coded safety rules stay in place and RL is used only where there is uncertainty, which speeds learning and cuts risk. RL rules can be created by chunking with an initial value from substate evaluation, then tuned by reward. Soar has no built-in intrinsic reward.
numbers: No new data. Intrinsic reward from appraisal theory exists only in an experimental version (Marinier 2009, cited).
limits: Overview paper. States that Soar has no automatic learning mechanism for semantic memory.
agent_relevance: Supports a hybrid: fixed guardrails as hard preferences, learned preferences only inside the leftover freedom.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to Soar, section 6 semantic memory
finding: Semantic memory holds context-free facts as graphs in the same form as working memory. Retrieval is by cue, with base-level activation (recency, frequency, noise) plus spreading activation from working memory. No automatic learning: the agent must store deliberately.
numbers: Why a separate store: cost of rule matching rises sharply with working memory size. Can be loaded from WordNet or DBpedia.
limits: No measured results in this section. Cited sources (Wang & Laird 2006; Derbinsky et al. 2010; Jones et al. 2016) not opened.
agent_relevance: Facts need an explicit write step. Spreading activation by context is the mechanism that picks the right sense of an ambiguous cue ('bank').

source: Soar Manual, chapter 6 Semantic Memory (activation and retrieval)
finding: Cue-based retrieval returns the matching long-term item with highest activation. Default is recency. Base-level activation uses the Petrov approximation of ACT-R. Spreading activation is additive on top of base level and flows along the stored graph.
numbers: Base-level k hard-coded to 10 stored boosts. Spreading-continue-probability default 0.9 (0.81 at depth 2). Spreading-limit default 300 items per source. Retrieval can prohibit specific items. Each retrieval creates a new short-term copy of the long-term item.
limits: Manual only. No behavioural data here.
agent_relevance: A 'prohibit' modifier is a clean way to ask for the next-best answer without repeating a rejected one. Useful for our retry step.

source: Soar Manual, chapter 7 Episodic Memory (retrieval formula)
finding: Episode match score = balance x cardinality + (1 - balance) x activation. Perfect-cardinality matches get a second structural graph match. Result is the most recent structural match or the most recent episode with best score. Retrieval can be limited with before/after/prohibit on time, and episodes can be stepped through.
numbers: Storage default: end of every decision cycle. SQLite store. Page size default 8192 bytes chosen from a test of 10 million decisions on a 2.8 GHz Core i7. Epmem and smem structures are excluded from storage by default.
limits: Manual only. Forgetting for episodic memory is not described as implemented in the version read.
agent_relevance: Recency tie-breaking is built into retrieval. For us: ties go to the newest record unless the cue says otherwise.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to Soar, section 7 episodic memory
finding: Episodes are automatic snapshots of the topstate, retrieved by partial-state cue with recency bias. Recent retrievals cost constant time, old ones slowly more. Laird lists uses: virtual sensing, action models from past operator effects, learning evaluation knowledge by retrospective analysis, prospective memory, and replay for debugging a past course of action.
numbers: No data. Cites Mohan & Laird 2013 (retrospective), Li & Laird 2015 (prospective), Jones & Laird 2019, Derbinsky et al. 2012; none opened.
limits: Author's own overview. Says episodic learning lacks generalisation but still helps.
agent_relevance: Retrospective analysis of a failed run to learn an operator evaluation is close to our 'revise from real output' guardrail G2.

source: Laird (2012) The Soar Cognitive Architecture, MIT Press
finding: The book that describes Soar 9 with RL, semantic and episodic memory added to procedural memory. The memory chapters are the source behind later summaries; I read the later summaries, not the book.
numbers: Not read. Facts about it come from Laird 2022 and the manual.
limits: Not opened this session. Treat any statement attributed only to the book as unverified here.
agent_relevance: Cite through Laird 2022 and the manual until the book is read.

source: Nason & Laird (2005) Soar-RL: integrating reinforcement learning with Soar, Cognitive Systems Research 6:51-59
finding: Original design of RL in Soar: numeric preferences on operators, updated by temporal difference. Source for RL rules. Only its metadata (about 159 citations on Semantic Scholar, closed access) was seen.
numbers: Not read. Citation count 159 from a Semantic Scholar search result seen this session.
limits: PDF not available. Its experiments and numbers are NOT recorded here.
agent_relevance: Open item: read it before claiming any quantitative RL result for Soar.

source: Derbinsky & Laird (2013) Effective and efficient forgetting in Soar's working and procedural memories; Derbinsky, Laird & Smith (2010) large declarative memories
finding: Known only as citations in the papers I read: the forgetting work covers working and procedural memory, not episodic memory. Not opened.
numbers: Not read. No numbers recorded.
limits: PDF not reachable (publisher returned 403 and search quota was exhausted). The 2012 Soar episodic memory description says forgetting is not included.
agent_relevance: Open item: forgetting policy for a growing record. See also Xiong 2025 below for LLM-agent evidence.

source: Lane, Morgan, Vickers, Woods & Nuxoll (2022) Towards an artificial, general episodic memory via learning in noisy, perceptually-aliased environments, ACS 10
finding: Phujus agent stores episodes as rules chained by internal sensors, to cope with perceptual aliasing and noise sensors. Claimed advantages over older agents NSM, MaRz and ARO: any number of sensors, no environment-specific tuning, better under a noise sensor.
numbers: Blind finite-state-machine task, three binary sensors (odd, noise with 50% chance on, one-state sensor). Result figures were not in the text I read; no numbers captured. Rule database grows exponentially, listed as the first future-work item.
limits: Short abstract-style paper. Authors call the evidence 'initial'. Their general-memory wish list includes an effective forgetting mechanism.
agent_relevance: Reminder that a growing record needs a size cap and removal of low-confidence entries before it is used for long runs.

source: Pink et al. (2025) Position: Episodic memory is the missing piece for long-term LLM agents
finding: Argues LLM agents need episodic memory with five properties: long-term storage, explicit reasoning over it, single-shot learning, instance-specific content, contextual relations. Says existing in-context, external and parametric methods each cover only some of them.
numbers: Position paper, no experiments.
limits: Argument, not evidence. Authors discuss alternative views where episodic memory is not needed.
agent_relevance: A checklist for judging our S0 record against the same five properties.

source: Wray, Kirk & Laird (2025) Applying cognitive design patterns to general LLM agents
finding: Compares Generative Agents memory to the Nuxoll-Laird list of episodic properties. It is automatic only partly, not episodically segmented, not deliberately cued, and relevance uses semantic similarity, not encoding specificity. Also notes that Reflexion caches reflections only within a task and that ExpeL needs a separate training stage, unlike Soar's online compilation.
numbers: Table 3 is qualitative: Automatic = Semi, Autonoetic = unknown, Episodic segmentation = No, Deliberate retrieval = No, Cue-based = Partial.
limits: Written by Soar authors, so a Soar-centred view. No new measurements.
agent_relevance: Names the gap our design could close: let the agent build its own cue and write its own record on a signal.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior
finding: Memory stream plus retrieval (recency, importance, relevance) plus reflection and planning. Ablating each part made believability rank lower.
numbers: 100 Prolific raters ranked 5 conditions. TrueSkill mean: full 29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, crowdworker 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21. Full vs fully ablated Cohen's d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4) = 150.29, p < 0.001. Recency decay factor 0.995 per hour.
limits: Believability ranked by humans, not task success. Agents sometimes embellish memories. Not a Soar-style episodic memory.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a retrieved record plus a periodic summary beats no record in an LLM agent, but the measure is human taste.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Agent stores short written lessons from failed attempts and reads them next trial. Gains on decision-making, QA and code. Isolating the lesson step: keeping just the last trajectory (episodic memory) helps less than writing a reflection.
numbers: ALFWorld 134 tasks: +22% absolute over baseline in 12 trials. HotPotQA +20%. HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% for GPT-4. Reflection adds 8% absolute over the episodic-trajectory-only condition. ReAct-only agent keeps a 22% hallucination rate. Memory size 3 experiences in ALFWorld.
limits: Same task repeated across trials, with a clear pass/fail signal. Lessons carry within a task, little across tasks (per Wray et al. 2025).
agent_relevance: A stored raw trace helps; a short distilled lesson helps more. Matches Soar's chunking of episodic results. Needs a real outcome signal.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: Skill library of verified code acts like procedural memory built online. Removing it makes progress plateau late. Removing self-verification cost most.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines. Wooden tools 15.3x faster. Random curriculum: item count down 93%. No self-verification: down 73%. Skill library removed: plateaus late in the run (no percentage in the text I read).
limits: Minecraft, three runs per tech-tree entry. Skills are code, a stricter record than free text.
agent_relevance: A record that is executable and checked before it is saved is worth more than free-text notes. Supports gating writes with a check.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: production-ready AI agents with scalable long-term memory (LoCoMo)
finding: An extract-and-update fact store beat chunk retrieval but lost to simply putting the full conversation in context on accuracy, while being much cheaper and faster.
numbers: LoCoMo overall J: Mem0 about 67%, Mem0 graph about 68%, best RAG about 61%, full context 72.9% at 26,031 tokens, with p95 total latency 17.1 s. Authors claim 26% relative gain over OpenAI memory, 91% lower p95 latency and over 90% token saving vs full context. Zep J 76.60 on one question type beats Mem0g 75.71.
limits: Vendor paper. Judge is an LLM. Full-context beat Mem0 on accuracy, so memory is a cost trade, not an accuracy gain.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: if the whole record fits in context, a memory layer may not help accuracy. It pays only when the record is too long.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: experience-following
finding: LLM agents copy the output of the retrieved memory most similar to the input. So wrong stored runs spread (error propagation), and correct-looking runs can still mislead (misaligned replay). Stricter admission and utility-based deletion helped.
numbers: Four agents tested (RegAgent, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT). Adding every run opens an immediate gap to an error-free-memory version and the gap grows. A strict evaluator before adding helps; history-based deletion is best with a strict evaluator; combined deletion cuts memory size the most. Exact success rates not reliably recoverable from the garbled tables.
limits: Four task sets. Findings depend on the evaluator quality used for admission.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to guardrail G3: only write to memory what passed a check on held-out input. Also supports pruning by retrieval utility.

source: Yan et al. (2026) Memory-R1: managing and using memory with reinforcement learning
finding: Trains a Memory Manager (ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, NOOP) and an Answer Agent with PPO or GRPO from outcome reward. This is RL on memory operations, the LLM version of Soar-RL controlling retrieval.
numbers: Only 152 training QA pairs. On LoCoMo with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, GRPO gives relative gains over Mem0 of 28% F1, 34% BLEU-1, 30% LLM-as-a-Judge. Also tested on MSC and LongMemEval, 3B to 14B models.
limits: Needs model training, which is outside our no-training rule. LLM judge. Gains are over one baseline.
agent_relevance: Confirms the Gorski-Laird idea (learn when to store and retrieve from reward) works with LLMs, but only by training. We can imitate it with fixed rules.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval: benchmarking chat assistants on long-term interactive memory (ICLR)
finding: 500 questions test extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, abstention. Commercial assistants and long-context models drop sharply when information must be kept over long chats.
numbers: Abstract: about a 30% accuracy drop for commercial chat assistants and long-context LLMs over sustained interactions. Design tweaks (session decomposition, fact-augmented keys, time-aware query expansion) raised recall.
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read. Benchmark is conversational, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: Knowledge update and abstention are listed memory skills. Our record needs a way to mark old facts as superseded.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan & Griffiths (2024) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA), TMLR
finding: Maps language agents onto Soar-style parts: working memory plus episodic, semantic and procedural long-term memory, with a decision loop. Says most retrieval-based systems use a fixed read-only semantic memory, and that language agents can also write new knowledge into it.
numbers: No experiments. Memory taxonomy only.
limits: Conceptual survey. Soar section follows Laird 2022.
agent_relevance: Gives us the vocabulary link: our S0 class record is an episodic or semantic write, chosen by code.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes & Laird (2022) Improving language model prompting in support of semi-autonomous task learning
finding: A Soar task-learning agent builds prompts for GPT-3 to get task steps it can parse and ground. Best setting was one prompt example and temperature 0.
numbers: Tidy a conference room: over 60% of responses were both situationally relevant and interpretable in the main test, over 80% at the best setting. Two other tasks: about 40% in main test, 60-80% reasonable at best.
limits: GPT-3 text-davinci-002, three tasks, human-judged. Old model.
agent_relevance: Shows an architecture agent using an LLM as a knowledge source and filtering by what its own memory can ground. Interpretability by the agent is a gate.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: natural language to generative symbolic rules for Soar via LLMs
finding: An LLM generator proposes Soar rules, runs them in Soar, and a critic revises from the real execution trace. Rules produced reached success rates over 86%. Removing the critic hurt most.
numbers: Water-jug dataset, Gemini and Qwen models. Gemini-Flash with the framework: 86% success rate, 1.76x minimum decision cycles; Gemini-Pro one-shot: 55% and about 2500x. Ablating critic: success down 23% (37% on hard cases); ablating basic knowledge base: down 17%; ablating case knowledge base: down 14%.
limits: One puzzle family. Authors' own benchmark. Procedural rules, not episodic memory.
agent_relevance: Execution-grounded critique beat model-only generation by a wide margin, which supports guardrail G2 (revise from real output).

source: Wray, Kirk & Laird (2021) Language models as a knowledge source for cognitive agents
finding: Reviews how a cognitive agent could pull task knowledge out of language models, and argues the agent should itself learn a model of what the LM knows.
numbers: No experiments.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Early statement of the pattern we use: LLM supplies content, architecture decides use.
